'''Joseph Ford''' (18 December 1927 – 26 April 1995) was [[Regents' Professor]] of physics at [[Georgia Institute of Technology]] specializing in [[thermodynamics]] and [[chaos theory]].<ref name=obit>{{cite journal|title=OBITUARIES Joseph Ford|issue=10 |pages=88 |journal=Physics Today|date=October 1995 |volume=48 |doi=10.1063/1.2808223|last1=Uzer |first1=T. |last2=Chirikov |first2=Boris |last3=Vivaldi |first3=Franco |last4=Casati |first4=Giulio |doi-access=free }}{{Dead link|date=May 2022 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Born in [[Buncombe County, North Carolina]], he was awarded a BS degree by the [[Georgia Institute of Technology]] in 1952 and a Ph.D  in physics by [[Johns Hopkins University]] in 1956.

==Career==
Ford spent two years as a research  physicist at [[Union Carbide Corporation]] in [[Niagara Falls, New York]] before joining the faculty at the [[University of Miami]] in 1958.  He was then appointed an associate professor at the [[Georgia Institute of Technology]] in 1961, rising to become Regents' Professor of Physics there in 1978, a position he held until his death in 1995.<ref name=obit/>

He was elected a [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]] in 1989 "for pioneering contributions in classical and quantal chaos, and for fundamental and significant contributions to theory of statistical mechanics, ergodicity, and stochasticity, and chaos"<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1989&unit_id=&institution=|title=APS Fellow Archive|publisher=APS|accessdate=3 October 2020}}</ref>

== Joseph Ford Commemorative Lectures ==
In 1995, the [[Georgia Institute of Technology School of Physics]] established the Joseph Ford Commemorative Lecture in honor of Ford's Memory.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.physics.gatech.edu/fordlecture | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130928220836/http://www.physics.gatech.edu/fordlecture | url-status=dead | archive-date=2013-09-28 |title=Annual Joseph Ford Commemorative Lecture }}</ref>
